etymology: Hebrew Dodo (H1734), his beloved or loving — from dod (H1730), beloved, an uncle; the word the bride uses of the bridegroom throughout the Song of Solomon.
biblical_def: Dodo was the father of two of David's fighting men and is named only as their father. Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite was one of the first three mighty men, who stood his ground against the Philistines at Pas-dammim when the men of Israel had gone away, and smote until his hand was weary and clave unto the sword (2Sa 23:9; 1Ch 11:12). Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem was one of the thirty (2Sa 23:24; 1Ch 11:26). The same or a related man appears as Dodai the Ahohite, set over the course of the second month in David's standing army, twenty-four thousand strong (1Ch 27:4). One household, then, supplied a man to the inner three and a man to the thirty. The name means his beloved, from dod, the tenderest word in the Hebrew vocabulary of affection — I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine (Son 6:3). It is an arresting name for the head of a house of soldiers, and it is not incongruous: the men who fought hardest for David were the men who loved him most, and Scripture never separates courage from affection.
webster_summary: Father of Eleazar, one of David's first three mighty men, and of Elhanan, one of the thirty; his name means his beloved.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that courage in Scripture grows out of love for a person, not out of abstract duty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Dodo is disputed by nobody. What his name quietly corrects is a cold view of Christian obedience — the notion that duty and affection are separate categories, and that the reliable soldier is the one who has stopped feeling anything. David's mighty men were not conscripts. They had come to him in the cave and the wilderness when he was a hunted man with nothing to give them, and what they did afterward at Pas-dammim and Bethlehem's well came out of that attachment.

The New Testament makes the connection the rule: If ye love me, keep my commandments (Joh 14:15); the love of Christ constraineth us (2Co 5:14); and the church at Ephesus, praised for labour and patience and hatred of evil doctrine, is nevertheless charged with having left its first love (Rev 2:2-4). Correct doctrine and hard work did not compensate for the loss. The principle to recover is that Christian valour is a form of love, that a man fights best for a Person he treasures, and that the house of his beloved sent its sons to the front for good reason.

etymology: Hebrew Elchanan (H445), God is gracious — from El (H410), God, and chanan (H2603), to be gracious, to show favour; the same root as Hannah, John and Hananiah.
biblical_def: Two men named Elhanan appear among David's warriors, and one of them stands at the centre of a famous question. The first is Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, listed among the thirty valiant men (2Sa 23:24; 1Ch 11:26). The second is the Elhanan of the Philistine wars, and here the two records must be read together. Second Samuel says that Elhanan the son of Jaareoregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam (2Sa 21:19, where the Authorized Version supplies the brother of in italics from the parallel); First Chronicles states it directly: Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1Ch 20:5). The Chronicler names the man Elhanan killed — Lahmi — and identifies him as Goliath's brother. David killed Goliath; Elhanan killed Goliath's brother. The name means God is gracious, and it is borne by men who fought giants: an apt confession for soldiers whose whole military theology was that the battle is the LORD's.
webster_summary: The name of David's warriors, including the Bethlehemite who slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite. It means God is gracious.
webster_full: ELHANAN, Hebrew Elchanan, God is gracious.
1. Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, one of the thirty valiant men of David.

The staff of Lahmi's spear was like a weaver's beam.
The father is called Jaare-oregim in the parallel passage of Samuel.

And there was again a battle in Gob with the Philistines, where Elhanan the son of Jaareoregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.

And there was war again with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam.
corruption_summary: The Elhanan passage is offered as proof that the David and Goliath story is legend; Chronicles names the man Elhanan actually killed, and it was Goliath's brother.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Samuel 21:19 is a standing exhibit in the case that the Old Testament preserves rival legends clumsily stitched together: on this reading, Elhanan originally killed Goliath, the tradition later transferred the feat to David for reasons of royal propaganda, and the Chronicler invented a brother named Lahmi to smooth over the embarrassment. Every step of that reconstruction is assumption rather than evidence. First Chronicles 20:5 is a text, not a later gloss on a text, and it contains a detail no harmoniser would invent: a personal name, Lahmi, for the man slain. Inventors remove difficulties; they do not add proper nouns that create new ones.

Nor is the Samuel reading difficult once the Hebrew is looked at. The Authorized Version prints the brother of in italics precisely to mark that the translators supplied it from the parallel, and the consonantal text of Samuel is readily accounted for as a transmissional variant of the fuller Chronicles reading. The dictionary's position on this class of case is the confessional one: the Scriptures were immediately inspired by God and are inerrant in the original autographs, and have been kept pure in all ages by His singular care and providence — which is why a variant like this is visible in the tradition rather than tidied out of it. What the two verses actually say, taken together, is plain: David killed Goliath, and one of David's men afterward killed Goliath's brother.

etymology: Hebrew Shammua (H8051), heard or renowned — from shama (H8085), to hear, to hearken, to obey; the verb of Hear, O Israel.
biblical_def: Four men in Scripture bear this name, and the first is the sobering one: Shammua the son of Zaccur, of the tribe of Reuben, was among the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan (Num 13:4), and therefore among the ten who brought back the evil report and died of the plague before the LORD. The best known is a son of David born in Jerusalem, named first in the list of the children of Bathsheba's house — Shammua, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon (2Sa 5:14; 1Ch 14:4; called Shimea at 1Ch 3:5). A Levite named Shammua is the ancestor of Abda who served in the temple after the return (Neh 11:17), and a priest of the house of Bilgah bore the name in Joiakim's day (Neh 12:18). The name means heard, from shama, and in Hebrew that verb never means bare hearing. It is the word of the Shema — Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD (Deu 6:4) — and to hear in that sense is to obey. That a man named heard stands among the spies who would not believe the report of God is the whole tragedy of Kadesh in one name.
webster_summary: The name of four men: a spy of the tribe of Reuben, a son of David born in Jerusalem, a Levite, and a priest. It means heard, or renowned.
webster_full: SHAMMUA, Hebrew Shammua, heard, renowned; from shama, to hear.
1. Son of Zaccur, of the tribe of Reuben, one of the twelve spies sent from Kadesh.
2. A son of David born unto him in Jerusalem; called Shimea in 1 Chronicles 3:5.
3. A Levite, ancestor of Abda who served after the return from Babylon.
4. A priest of the house of Bilgah in the days of Joiakim.
scriptures: And these be the names of those that were born unto him in Jerusalem; Shammua, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon,
Now these are the names of his children which he had in Jerusalem; Shammua, and Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon,
And these were born unto him in Jerusalem; Shimea, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon, four, of Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel:
Of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jehonathan;
corruption_summary: Hearing is reduced to information received; the Hebrew verb means hearing that obeys, and the New Testament keeps the same standard.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture with unlimited access to preaching has quietly redefined hearing as consumption. Sermons are streamed, conferences attended, doctrine discussed, and the transaction is felt to be complete when the content has been understood and approved. Hebrew will not allow the split. Shama means to hear and to heed with one motion, which is why the same word is translated hear, hearken and obey throughout the Old Testament, and why Samuel could say to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams (1Sa 15:22) using this very verb.

James states it for the church without softening: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves (Jas 1:22), and the deception is self-inflicted — a man who has listened attentively feels he has done something. The spies at Kadesh had heard everything: the promise, the covenant, the report of the land. Ten of them saw the giants and would not go up, and the generation died in the wilderness because the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it (Heb 4:2). The principle to recover is that a sermon is not finished when it is understood; it is finished when it is done.

etymology: Hebrew Shobab (H7727), turned back, backsliding, or rebellious — from shub (H7725), to turn, to return; the same verb that means both to backslide and to repent, according to the direction of the turning.
biblical_def: Shobab was a son of David born in Jerusalem, second in the list of the sons of Bathsheba's house — Shammua, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon (2Sa 5:14; 1Ch 3:5; 1Ch 14:4). A second Shobab appears in Judah's genealogy as a son of Caleb (1Ch 2:18). The name is built on shub, and that root is the most morally loaded verb in the Hebrew Bible, because it faces both ways. Turned one direction it is backsliding: Turn, O backsliding children, saith the LORD (Jer 3:14), where the word rendered backsliding is this word. Turned the other it is repentance itself: Turn ye even to me with all your heart (Joe 2:12); Let the wicked forsake his way… and let him return unto the LORD (Isa 55:7). One verb, two destinations, and everything depends on which way a man's face is set. That such a name sits in the middle of the list of David's Jerusalem-born sons, in a household that knew both the depth of the king's fall and the reality of his restoration, is a fitting accident of the record.
webster_summary: A son of David born in Jerusalem, and a son of Caleb in the genealogy of Judah; the name is built on the verb to turn.
webster_full: SHOBAB, Hebrew Shobab, turned back, backsliding, rebellious.
1. A son of David, born unto him in Jerusalem.
Named with Shammua, Nathan and Solomon among the sons of Bathsheba's house.
2. A son of Caleb in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
From shub, to turn or return, the verb of both backsliding and repentance.
scriptures: And these be the names of those that were born unto him in Jerusalem; Shammua, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon,
And these were born unto him in Jerusalem; Shimea, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon, four, of Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel:
Now these are the names of his children which he had in Jerusalem; Shammua, and Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon,
Jer 3:22
Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: Repentance is softened into regret or reframed as growth; the Hebrew verb means an about-turn, and it is the same word as backsliding reversed.
corruption_paragraphs: Two substitutes for repentance are current. The first is regret — genuine sorrow over consequences, which Scripture distinguishes sharply from the real thing: godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death (2Co 7:10). Judas was sorry. The second substitute is the language of growth and process, in which a man is always becoming and never turning, and sin is a stage rather than a direction. Neither substitute contains the idea that shub actually carries, which is a change of direction: stopping, facing the other way, and walking back.

Because the verb is the same in both directions, the Old Testament can put the whole gospel appeal in a single line of wordplay — Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings (Jer 3:22). The man who has turned away is called to turn back by the same motion that took him off, and the healing is promised to the turning. The principle to recover is that repentance is a change of course rather than a change of feeling, that it is commanded of all men everywhere (Act 17:30), and that the God who names the disease is the one offering to heal it.

etymology: Hebrew Malkishua (H4444), my king is salvation — from melek (H4428), king, and yasha (H3467), to save, to deliver; written Melchishua at 1 Samuel 14:49.
biblical_def: Malchishua was a son of King Saul, named with Jonathan, Ishui and Abinadab in the royal genealogy (1Sa 14:49, where the Authorized Version spells it Melchishua; 1Ch 8:33; 9:39). He died with his father and brothers on Mount Gilboa when the Philistines overtook the house of Saul, and Israel's first dynasty ended in a single day on a hillside. Nothing else is told of him — no word, no act, no judgment passed on his character. He is a son who fell with his father. The name is the sharpest thing about him: my king is salvation. Saul named his sons as a believing Israelite named sons, with confessions — Jonathan, the LORD has given; Malchishua, my king is salvation; Eshbaal and Meribbaal, names later prudently altered by the chroniclers. The confession in Malchishua's name is true, and the tragedy is what Saul made of it. The king he had in view was, in the end, himself; and the reign that began with a man head and shoulders above the people ended with the sons of that house dead on Gilboa. Only the King who is Himself the salvation of His people saves those who die with Him.
webster_summary: A son of King Saul, slain with his father and brothers on Mount Gilboa; his name means my king is salvation.
webster_full: MALCHISHUA, Hebrew Malkishua, my king is salvation; written Melchishua in 1 Samuel.
A son of Saul the first king of Israel.
Named with Jonathan, Ishui and Abinadab among the sons of Saul.
He fell with his father and his brethren in the battle on mount Gilboa.
From melek, a king, and yasha, to save.
scriptures: Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchishua: and the names of his two daughters were these; the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal:
And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
And the Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul's sons.
And Ner begat Kish; and Kish begat Saul; and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
corruption_summary: Salvation is claimed by association — family, church, heritage; Scripture makes it personal union with the King who saves.
corruption_paragraphs: Malchishua carried a true confession in his name, was born into the royal house of Israel, was brother to Jonathan whom Scripture honours, and died on Gilboa under his father's ruin. His case presses the question that every covenant community must keep asking: whether nearness to the things of God is the same as salvation. It is not. They are not all Israel, which are of Israel (Rom 9:6). A man may be the son of a king of Israel, bear a name that says my king is salvation, and be buried under the judgment that fell on his house.

This is not to pronounce on Malchishua's soul, of which Scripture says nothing and about which the dictionary will say nothing. It is to name the false inference — that proximity saves. The Lord Jesus warned that many would say Lord, Lord and be told I never knew you (Mat 7:22-23), and He said it to religious people with impeccable connections. The principle to recover is that the King who is salvation saves persons, one at a time, by uniting them to Himself through faith; and that the most orthodox name in Israel, worn without that union, is a sentence a man does not possess.

etymology: Hebrew Miqloth (H4732), staves or rods — a plural form from a root signifying a staff or rod.
biblical_def: Two men bear this name. The first is a Benjamite of the house of Jehiel the father of Gibeon, in the genealogy that runs down to Saul: Mikloth begat Shimeah, and these dwelt with their brethren in Jerusalem, over against them (1Ch 8:32; 9:37-38). The second is an officer in David's standing army: over the course of the second month was Dodai an Ahohite, and of his course was Mikloth also the ruler: in his course likewise were twenty and four thousand (1Ch 27:4). The chapter he stands in is one of the most administratively dull in Scripture and one of the most instructive: David divided the men of Israel into twelve courses of twenty-four thousand, each course serving one month in the year, so that the kingdom was defended continuously without any man being under arms all year. Mikloth was the second-in-command of the second month. His name means staves, and a staff in Scripture is both the shepherd's instrument and the emblem of rule — thy rod and thy staff they comfort me (Psa 23:4). It is a good name for a man whose work was to hold a rota together.
webster_summary: A Benjamite of the house of Gibeon in Saul's genealogy, and the ruler under Dodai over the course of the second month in David's army.
webster_full: MIKLOTH, Hebrew Miqloth, staves, rods.
1. A Benjamite of the house of Jehiel the father of Gibeon, father of Shimeah.
His house dwelt with their brethren in Jerusalem, over against them.
2. The ruler in the course of the second month of David's army.
That course, under Dodai the Ahohite, numbered twenty and four thousand.
scriptures: And Mikloth begat Shimeah. And these also dwelt with their brethren in Jerusalem, over against them.
And Gedor, and Ahio, and Zechariah, and Mikloth.
And over the course of the second month was Dodai an Ahohite, and of his course was Mikloth also the ruler: in his course likewise were twenty and four thousand.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that good order is a spiritual matter, and rotas are a form of mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mikloth has no critics. What his chapter corrects is a persistent piety that treats administration as the unspiritual part of church life — the rota, the schedule, the division of labour, all tolerated as necessary evils while the real work goes on elsewhere. David did not think so, and the Holy Ghost gave a chapter of Chronicles to the arrangement: twelve courses, twenty-four thousand men each, one month apiece, year after year.

Consider what the system did for the men in it. No soldier was permanently away from his fields and his household; every man knew which month was his; the kingdom was never undefended; and no one was indispensable. That is not bureaucracy, it is care. The New Testament carries the same instinct: the apostles appointed seven over the daily ministration so that the widows were not neglected and the word was not left (Act 6:1-4); elders are appointed in every city (Tit 1:5); and the whole chapter on the most spectacular gifts ends let all things be done decently and in order (1Co 14:40). The principle to recover is that faithful structure is how love gets delivered reliably rather than occasionally.

etymology: Hebrew Nimshi (H5250), commonly read rescued or drawn out, from a root signifying to draw out — the same idea that stands behind the name of Moses, because I drew him out of the water (Exo 2:10).
biblical_def: Nimshi is known entirely through his grandson. Jehu, the captain who destroyed the house of Ahab and cut down the worship of Baal in Israel, is called Jehu the son of Nimshi so consistently that the grandfather's name almost serves as the family surname, even where the father Jehoshaphat is also named: look out there Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi (2Ki 9:2). The commission was given to Elijah at Horeb — Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel (1Ki 19:16) — and carried out a generation later by Elisha's servant. And the house gave Israel one of the most vivid lines in the Old Testament, the watchman's report from the tower of Jezreel: the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously (2Ki 9:20). Nimshi himself does nothing in Scripture. What he has is a name attached to a judgment that God had announced through Elijah and did not forget for years, and the record is that the LORD keeps His word across generations that have no idea they are carrying it.
webster_summary: Grandfather of Jehu king of Israel, whose name is the standing designation of Jehu throughout Kings and Chronicles.
webster_full: NIMSHI, Hebrew Nimshi, commonly read rescued or drawn out.
Grandfather of Jehu, the captain whom the LORD raised up to destroy the house of Ahab.
Jehu is repeatedly called the son of Nimshi, even where his father Jehoshaphat is named.
The commission to anoint Jehu was first given to Elijah at Horeb.
The watchman of Jezreel knew the house by its driving: he driveth furiously.
scriptures: And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.
And when thou comest thither, look out there Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in, and make him arise up from among his brethren, and carry him to an inner chamber;
And the watchman told, saying, He came even unto them, and cometh not again: and the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously.
And the destruction of Ahaziah was of God by coming to Joram: for when he was come, he went out with Jehoram against Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab.
corruption_summary: Delay in God's judgment is taken for indifference; the word spoken to Elijah at Horeb was executed a generation later, exactly as given.
corruption_paragraphs: When judgment does not fall promptly, men conclude that it will not fall — Where is the promise of his coming? (2Pe 3:4), and because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil (Ecc 8:11). The house of Ahab had every reason to draw that conclusion. Elijah received the commission concerning Jehu at Horeb, and then Elijah died, and Ahab died, and years passed under Joram, and nothing happened. The delay was not forgetfulness. Peter gives the reason for such intervals: the Lord is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance (2Pe 3:9).

When the word did come due it came exactly as spoken, through a prophet's servant with a box of oil, and the whole house of Ahab fell in a few days. The same principle governs the last judgment, which Scripture treats as certain precisely because a day is appointed (Act 17:31). The principle to recover is that God's patience is not His approval, and that a word of His spoken to one generation is still live ammunition in the next. Jehu's grandfather never knew what his family name would be attached to.
roots_lines: Hebrew Nimshi (H5250) — grandfather of Jehu; 1 Kings 19:16, 2 Kings 9:2, 9:20, 2 Chronicles 22:7.
Hebrew mashah (H4871) — to draw out; because I drew him out of the water (Exo 2:10).
Hebrew Yehu (H3058) — Jehu, the LORD is He; the king raised up against the house of Ahab.
Hebrew mashach (H4886) — to anoint; the act commanded to Elijah and performed by Elisha's servant.
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patience; the reason judgment tarries (2Pe 3:9).

“Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi”.
“The driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously”.

etymology: Hebrew Yehozabad (H3075), the LORD has endowed or the LORD has given — from Yah, the covenant name, and zabad (H2064), to bestow, to endow with a gift.
biblical_def: Three men bear this name, and the first stands under a shadow. Jehozabad the son of Shomer was one of the two servants who conspired against Joash king of Judah and slew him on his bed (2Ki 12:21); the Chronicler adds the detail that his mother Shimrith was a Moabitess (2Ch 24:26), and gives the reason the servants rose: Joash had murdered Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, the man whose father had saved his life and set him on the throne, and had done it in the court of the house of the LORD (2Ch 24:20-22). The second Jehozabad was a son of Obed-edom, second of the porters at the house of God, of a family famed for faithfulness at a door (1Ch 26:4). The third was a Benjamite captain under Jehoshaphat with a hundred and eighty thousand men ready prepared for the war (2Ch 17:18). The name means the LORD has given, and the three men together show how differently a gift may be spent: one used his position to kill a king, one kept a gate, one held a command.
webster_summary: The name of three men: a servant who slew Joash king of Judah, a son of Obed-edom among the porters, and a captain under Jehoshaphat.
webster_full: JEHOZABAD, Hebrew Yehozabad, the LORD has endowed, or the LORD has given.
1. Son of Shomer, or of Shimrith a Moabitess; one of the servants who slew Joash king of Judah.
Joash had slain Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, the priest who preserved him.
2. Jehozabad the second son of Obed-edom, among the porters of the house of God.
3. A captain of Benjamin under Jehoshaphat, with an hundred and fourscore thousand men.
scriptures: For Jozachar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him, and he died; and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David: and Amaziah his son reigned in his stead.
And these are they that conspired against him; Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith a Moabitess.
Moreover the sons of Obededom were, Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, and Sacar the fourth, and Nethaneel the fifth,
And next him was Jehozabad, and with him an hundred and fourscore thousand ready prepared for the war.
corruption_summary: A just cause is taken to justify any means; the murder of Joash was real judgment on a real crime and was itself avenged as murder.
corruption_paragraphs: The end of Joash is a hard passage handled carelessly by both kinds of reader. One kind treats the servants as instruments of divine justice and effectively approves the assassination: Joash had murdered the prophet who rebuked him, the son of the very priest who hid him from Athaliah, and Zechariah had died saying The LORD look upon it, and require it (2Ch 24:22). The other kind reads the whole episode as pure court intrigue with no moral shape at all. Scripture holds both truths without blurring them. The Chronicler frames the conspiracy as the consequence of the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and the LORD did require it.

Yet Amaziah, Joash's son, executed the servants who killed his father (2Ki 14:5-6), and Scripture records it as a lawful act, done according to the law of Moses and without touching their children. Both things stand: God used the murder as judgment, and the murderers were guilty of murder. This is exactly the pattern of Acts 2:23, where Christ is delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and the men who did it are charged with having taken, and by wicked hands… crucified and slain Him. The principle to recover is that God's sovereign use of a wicked act never makes the act less wicked, and no man may plead providence as a defence for what he chose to do.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yehozabad (H3075), from Yah and zabad (H2064), to bestow, to endow.
roots_lines: Hebrew zabad (H2064) — to bestow, to endow with a gift; Leah's word at the birth of Zebulun (Gen 30:20).
Hebrew Yehozabad (H3075) — borne by three men; 2 Kings 12:21, 1 Chronicles 26:4, 2 Chronicles 17:18, 24:26.
Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to conspire, to bind together; the verb of the plot against Joash.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to require; The LORD look upon it, and require it (2Ch 24:22).
Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, determinate purpose; delivered by the determinate counsel… of God (Act 2:23).
usage: “Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him, and he died”.
“Jehozabad the second” — among the sons of Obed-edom the porter.
“And next him was Jehozabad, and with him an hundred and fourscore thousand ready prepared for the war”.

etymology: Hebrew Abdi (H5660), my servant — from ebed (H5650), a servant, a bondman, one who serves; the word in Behold my servant, whom I uphold (Isa 42:1).
biblical_def: Abdi is a Levitical name of the house of Merari. The first is an ancestor of Ethan the singer, who stood on the left hand in the service of song that David set over the house of the LORD: Ethan the son of Kishi, the son of Abdi, the son of Malluch (1Ch 6:44). The second is the father of Kish, one of the Levites who arose when Hezekiah opened the doors of the house of the LORD and set about cleansing it — a roll-call of the men who did the unglamorous work of carrying out the filthiness from the holy place (2Ch 29:12). The third is one of the sons of Elam who had taken strange wives and put them away at Ezra's reformation (Ezr 10:26). The name means simply my servant. In Scripture that is not a small thing to be called. It is the title God gives Moses, David, Isaiah, Israel, and supremely the Messiah in Isaiah's Servant Songs; and it is the name the Lord Jesus took when He made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant (Php 2:7).
webster_summary: A Levitical name of the house of Merari: an ancestor of Ethan the singer, the father of Kish under Hezekiah, and a son of Elam in Ezra's day.
webster_full: ABDI, Hebrew Abdi, my servant; from ebed, a servant.
1. A Levite of the sons of Merari, ancestor of Ethan the singer.
2. Father of Kish, one of the Levites who cleansed the house of the LORD under Hezekiah.
3. One of the sons of Elam who had taken a strange wife in the days of Ezra.
The word ebed is the title given to Moses, David and the Messiah.
scriptures: And their brethren the sons of Merari stood on the left hand: Ethan the son of Kishi, the son of Abdi, the son of Malluch,

Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:
And of the sons of Elam; Mattaniah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, and Abdi, and Jeremoth, and Eliah.
Isa 42:1
Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.
corruption_summary: Servanthood is treated as beneath the dignity of a free man; Scripture makes it the highest title God confers and the form Christ Himself took.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears servant as a diminishment and bondservant as an outrage, and a Christianity that speaks of belonging to a Master is heard as an assault on autonomy. Scripture's valuation is the reverse. Moses my servant is dead (Jos 1:2) is spoken as an honour; David my servant is the LORD's standing designation for the king; and the highest of all the Servant Songs opens Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth (Isa 42:1). The word is not a demotion. It is what it looks like to belong to God.

The apostles chose the title for themselves without embarrassment: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle (Rom 1:1), using the word for a bondslave. And they had a reason. The alternative to being Christ's servant is not freedom but another master — his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness (Rom 6:16). The principle to recover is that every man serves something, that the only liberty available is the liberty of the right Master, and that a Levite named my servant was carrying a better title than most kings.
roots_summary: Hebrew Abdi (H5660), from ebed (H5650), a servant, a bondman.
roots_lines: Hebrew ebed (H5650) — a servant, a bondman; the title of Moses, David, Israel and the Messiah.
Hebrew Abdi (H5660) — a Levite of Merari; 1 Chronicles 6:44, 2 Chronicles 29:12, Ezra 10:26.
Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, to serve, to worship; service and worship are one verb.
Hebrew Merari (H4847) — the Levitical house that bore the boards and sockets of the tabernacle.
Greek doulos (G1401) — a bondservant; took upon him the form of a servant (Php 2:7).
usage: “Ethan the son of Kishi, the son of Abdi, the son of Malluch”.
“Of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi” — at Hezekiah's cleansing.
“Behold my servant, whom I uphold” (Isa 42:1).

etymology: Hebrew Adiel (H5717), ornament of God — from adi (H5716), an ornament, jewellery, that which adorns, and El (H410), God.
biblical_def: Three men bear this name. The first is a prince of Simeon, named among those whose families increased greatly and who went to seek pasture at Gedor (1Ch 4:36). The second is a priest, father of Maasiai, in the roll of those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity (1Ch 9:12). The third holds one of the most trusted posts in David's kingdom: over the king's treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel (1Ch 27:25). The name means ornament of God, from adi, the word for jewellery and adornment, and it sits well beside a son entrusted with the royal treasury. Scripture has a settled doctrine about ornament, and it is not that beauty is suspect. God Himself adorned His bride: I decked thee also with ornaments… and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom (Eze 16:11-13). What Scripture insists on is where the adorning is done. Peter directs wives away from the plaiting of hair and wearing of gold to the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price (1Pe 3:4).
webster_summary: The name of three men: a prince of Simeon, a priest of the return, and the father of Azmaveth who was over David's treasures.
webster_full: ADIEL, Hebrew Adiel, ornament of God.
1. A prince of the tribe of Simeon in the days of Hezekiah.
2. A priest, father of Maasiai, among those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity.
3. Father of Azmaveth, who was over the king's treasures in the reign of David.
From adi, an ornament or jewel, with El, God.
scriptures: And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah,
And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;
And over the king's treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah:
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Beauty is either worshipped or suspected; Scripture calls it a good gift and locates the adorning that lasts in the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The age is at war with itself about appearance. It spends more on adorning the body than any civilisation before it while insisting that appearance should not matter, and it hands young women a standard no one can meet and then calls the resulting misery a private failure. The church's answer has too often been the ascetic one — treating attention to beauty as vanity by definition — which is not what Scripture says and which no one believes for long.

The Bible is unembarrassed about beauty. God made Eve and Adam sang; the tabernacle was built with gold and blue and purple and scarlet and fine twined linen, beautiful by divine specification; and in Ezekiel 16 it is the LORD who decks His bride with ornaments. What Peter does is not abolish adornment but relocate its centre of gravity: not the outward plaiting of the hair, but let it be the hidden man of the heart… even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price (1Pe 3:3-4). The principle to recover is proportion. A woman who has spent nothing on the imperishable ornament has nothing that will last, and a church that scolds about clothing while neglecting the heart has copied the world's mistake with the sign reversed.
roots_summary: Hebrew Adiel (H5717), from adi (H5716), an ornament, with El (H410), God.

Hebrew otsar (H214) — a treasure, a storehouse; the charge of Azmaveth the son of Adiel.
Hebrew tiphereth (H8597) — beauty, glory, adorning; used of the priestly garments, for glory and for beauty (Exo 28:2).
Greek kosmos (G2889) — adornment, order; the root of the New Testament verb to adorn (1Ti 2:9).
usage: “Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah” — princes of Simeon.
“Maasiai the son of Adiel” — among the priests at Jerusalem.
“Over the king's treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel”.
